newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rally on mild inflation, dollar weaker.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rally on mild inflation, dollar weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks posted their second biggest one-day gain ever on Tuesday as bonds rallied on signs that retail inflation remained under control.
The dollar fell against the German mark on profit-taking.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended with a gain of 135.26 points, or 2.10 percent, at 6,587.16 -- the next best gain in point terms after soaring 187 points on Oct. 21, 1987, or two days after the "Black Monday" crash that wiped out 508 points from the Dow.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,840 to 764 on active volume of 506 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The 30-stock Dow index -- the world's most closely watched stock index -- has been on the comeback trail since Monday, when it jumped 60 points, and has erased more than a quarter of the nearly 700-point decline it posted after setting its last record high close of 7,085.16 on March 11.
Investors were relieved that the Consumer Price Index for March did not confirm the inflationary pressures suggested in Friday's Producer Price Index report.
The inflation report had kept investors on edge, particularly in light of a 148-point sell-off in the Dow last Friday on the unexpected 0.4 percent rise in wholesale prices.
"It's a sigh of relief that our worst fears were not materialised," said John Church, chief investment officer at the Glenmede Trust Co.

The Labour Department said the CPI rose 0.1 percent in March, after rising 0.3 percent in February. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the index rose only 0.2 percent after being up the same amount in February.
The bond market also was buoyed by Tuesday's inflation data. The Treasury's 30-year bond gained nearly a full point, and its yield tumbled to 7.09 percent from Monday's close of 7.17 percent.
Strong earnings from Dow components Caterpillar Inc. and Eastman Kodak Co. were both among the companies reporting earnings that exceeded Wall Street estimates.
"My argument has been that strong earnings should provide the antidote for this market," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "So far they are."
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.7270 marks, down from 1.7310 marks on Monday. The dollar fell to 126.07 Japanese yen from 126.63 yen.

Gold for June delivery at the Commodity Exchange ended $4.80 lower at $343.90 an ounce, as speculators sold gold -- a traditional hedge against inflation -- following the surprisingly mild consumer price data.

Oil prices fell as concerns about tensions with Iran faded and amid amid expectations of rising crude oil stocks. At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for May delivery ended 7 cents a barrel lower at $19.83.

Heating oil for May delivery closed 0.18 cent a gallon higher at 54.85 cents, supported by cold weather in much of the United States. May unleaded gasoline closed down 0.06 cent a gallon at 61.90 cents.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee prices closed lower on expectations that physical coffee stocks would show a big rise in a monthly report by the Green Coffee Association of New York.
Coffee for May delivery closed 3.60 cents a pound lower at 192.40 cents after trading as high as 201.50 cents early.
Overseas, London's benchmark FTSE 100 index closed 35.1 points higher at 4,286.8. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average climbed 241.12 points to finish at 17,933.59.
